28292:
Elijah the Tishbite bursts into the story unannounced to confront Ahab and Jezebel's promotion of Baal, the storm and fertility god, with a drought that only the LORD can end. His ministry is one long argument that the LORD alone is God, climaxing on Mount Carmel when fire falls on his sacrifice after Baal's prophets have cried out all day in vain.

The story also shows his human frailty. Immediately after Carmel he flees from Jezebel's threat, asks to die, and is gently restored by God at Horeb, the mountain of Moses, where God speaks in a low whisper and gives him new work: anointing kings and a successor, Elisha. He is one of two people in the Old Testament who do not die but are taken by God, carried up in a whirlwind.

Malachi's promise that Elijah would return before the day of the LORD made him a figure of expectation. The Gospels identify John the Baptist as the Elijah who was to come, and Elijah himself appears with Moses at the transfiguration of Jesus.
28293: A Tishbite from Gilead (1 Kgs 17:1), hairy and wearing a leather belt (2 Kgs 1:8). Announced drought, was fed by ravens and a widow, raised her son, defeated Baal's prophets on Carmel, fled to Horeb, called Elisha, condemned Ahab and Ahaziah, and was taken up by a whirlwind (2 Kgs 2:11). 2 Chr 21:12-15 records a letter from him to Jehoram of Judah. Malachi promises his return (Mal 4:5); Jesus identifies John the Baptist with that role (Matt 11:14; 17:12). James calls him a man with a nature like ours (Jas 5:17).
28294: Elijah is the herald of the Messiah. A cup is poured for him at the Passover Seder and a chair set for him at circumcisions; he is expected to resolve unanswered legal questions. Rabbinic stories show him appearing to sages and the poor.
28295: Honoured as a saint (20 July). The Carmelite order looks to him as spiritual founder. Many fathers taught that Elijah and Enoch are the two witnesses of Rev 11 who will return before the end.
28296: Most Protestants hold that Malachi's prophecy was fulfilled in John the Baptist, who came 'in the spirit and power of Elijah' (Luke 1:17); some dispensationalists expect a future literal return as one of the two witnesses.
28297: The Elijah cycle is usually seen as prophetic legends from northern circles, incorporated into Kings, with the Carmel story as polemic against Baal's claim to control rain and fire. Scholars debate the Chronicler's letter to Jehoram, since 2 Kgs 3:11 suggests Elijah had already gone.

28364:
Elisha son of Shaphat was Elijah's disciple and successor, called from the plough at Abel-meholah. When Elijah was taken up, Elisha received his cloak and a double portion of his spirit, and he went on to a long ministry of about fifty years through the reigns of several northern kings.

Where Elijah was a solitary figure of confrontation, Elisha often worked among the communities of the 'sons of the prophets', and many of his miracles meet ordinary needs: a widow's debts, a poisoned pot, a lost axe-head, a childless woman, a dead son. He also acted on the international stage, advising kings in war, healing the Aramean commander Naaman, foretelling Hazael's rule in Damascus, and setting Jehu's coup in motion.

His miracles of multiplying bread and raising the dead are widely seen as anticipations of Jesus' ministry, and Jesus cites his healing of the foreigner Naaman as a sign of God's grace to the Gentiles.
28365: Son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah, anointed to succeed Elijah (1 Kgs 19:16). Received a double portion of Elijah's spirit (2 Kgs 2:9-15). Performed many miracles (2 Kgs 2-8), anointed Jehu through a disciple (2 Kgs 9:1-3), died in the reign of Joash of Israel (2 Kgs 13:14-20). Jesus mentions Naaman's healing (Luke 4:27).

28367: Honoured as a saint (14 June in many calendars). His miracles are read typologically: the Jordan cleansing of Naaman as baptism, the feeding of a hundred as foreshadowing the feeding of the multitudes, the raising by his bones as related to the veneration of relics.
28368: Elisha is generally presented as a model of faithful discipleship and succession, and his miracles as signs of God's care amid apostasy. The bear episode is explained by many as judgment on a mob of young men mocking God's prophet, rather than on small children.
28369: The Elisha cycle is usually seen as a collection of prophetic legends from northern prophetic guilds, with some stories possibly transferred between Elijah and Elisha. Scholars note its chronological placement is loose (e.g. 2 Kgs 8:1-6 after Gehazi's leprosy).

28496: Uzziah (also called Azariah) ruled Judah for fifty-two years in the eighth century BC, a long, prosperous reign that paralleled Jeroboam II in the north. Chronicles portrays a capable builder, farmer and soldier who expanded Judah's reach toward Edom and Philistia, but whose pride led him to usurp the priestly office of burning incense; he spent his last years with a skin disease while his son Jotham acted as regent. His death frames Isaiah's call, and the prophetic books of Hosea and Amos are dated by his reign.
